catalog_quote: 2.1.3. Tonal System in Kono Language The below tones are used in kono to create differences in meaning of words that have the same form. They could also have syntactic significance. Kono language makes use of three distinctive level tones, which are; High tone ( /) Mid tone (unmarked) Low tone ( \) High tone ... kashákúrá [kaʃákúrá] ‘old person’ ... géliljà [gélilʤá] ‘sew’ ... gópọbú [gpɔbú] ‘roast’ ... Mid tone ... ga [ga] ‘lose’ ... moji [moʤi] ‘ground’ ... Low tone ... gosho [gòʃò] ‘weep’ ... kugbit [kùgbìt] ‘ear’ ... mọ [m] ‘water’ ... THE SYLLABLE STRUCTURE Kono language operates the syllable structure that can be described as cv, vcvcv, vcv, cvcv, cvcvcv, and cvcvv.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kono is described as a tone language with three lexically contrastive level tones (High, Mid, Low); the source says nothing at all about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None; no stress discussion exists in the source.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on words in citation form (elicited via frame technique from two speakers from Zampuru, Kauru LGA, resident in Saminaka). Source is an undergraduate long essay whose main topic is syntax; the phonology chapter is brief and tone marking in the data is inconsistent, so treat as low-authority.
new_statements.identity_note: Bakare 2011 is unambiguously Kono of Kauru LGA, Kaduna State (informants from Zampuru, resident in Saminaka), i.e. kono1264 / klk, not Kono of Sierra Leone (Mande) or Kono of Guinea. No dialect distinctions are made.

sources.note: Ch. 2 'Basic phonological/syntactic concepts' gives consonant and vowel inventories, sec. 2.1.3 'Tonal System in Kono Language' (p. 40): three distinctive level tones H, M (unmarked), L with lexical (and possibly syntactic) function; sec. 2.1.4 syllable structure. No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the essay (a full-text search for stress/accent full text: 'stress' occurs only in 'distress').

sources.note: Phonology section (3.1) describes Boze only (four level tones plus glides); Kono appears only in Table 1 with status '?' ('no information'), in the family tree, and with one lexical item (u-ʧara 'arm'). Nothing on Kono prosody; nothing on stress for any East Kainji language.
